newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire doesn't stop fight as rebel deadline ends.
newsitem.headline: Zaire doesn't stop fight as rebel deadline ends.

text.p: A rebel deadline for Zairean soldiers to give up their weapons passes on Thursday with both sides preparing for a showdown over the eastern garrison city of Kisangani.

Zaire's Prime Minister, Kengo wa Dondo, denounced foreign indifference as international pressure builds for some kind of intervention, and the U.N. refugee agency said hunger and disease were killing frightened Hutu refugees hiding in the eastern rainforest.

Rebel radio in Goma reported the fall of Kongolo, 700 km (440 miles) to the south, at a crossing on the Zaire river and said rebel troops were close to reaching the diamond-rich opposition heartland of Kasai.
"The town of Kongolo was captured without a fight because soldiers have left to reinforce Kisangani, which is surrounded by the Alliance," the Voice of the People said.
But residents of Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city, reported an uneasy calm there, saying that any fighting between the army and advancing rebels was out of earshot.
The Alliance of Democratic Forces last week gave the army until March 13 to lay down their weapons.

"I find it regrettable that the international community through the United Nations through the United States and Britain gives the impression that the tragedy unfolding in Zaire doesn't interest them," Kengo told a news conference on Wednesday.
"Perhaps because it is a question of Africans," he added.
He warned that the collapse of Zaire would rebound on the whole region but said that if Zaire's sovereignty was respected, a political solution was possible.
"Before going to elections, we can solve the nationality problems at the centre of this debate," he said.
The Tutsi-led rebels, who hold most of the east, took up arms in October after local officials threatened to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home.
They say they want to topple veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko, who is in Europe where he has spent most of his time since having prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland in August.
Zaire accuses neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of invading in support of the rebels.
In Goma representatives of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said that Hutus too weak to flee eastern camps were dying from disease and hunger as thousands more hide in nearby forests.
"We got a report that 35 people have died within three days," Craig Sanders said after visiting Tingi Tingi and Amisi.
U.N. agencies on Wednesday supplied biscuits and blankets to the camps, which may be used as staging posts for the repatriation of the refugees to Rwanda and Burundi.
Around 170,000 refugees fled Tingi Tingi before it was captured on February 1.

While rebels have now moved on towards their stated target of Kisangani, 250 km (160 miles) to the northwest, many of the refugees have fled towards Ubundu on the Zaire river 100 km (60 miles) south of Kisangani.
With Kisangani residents reporting an uneasy calm, the defence ministry in Kinshasa reported that the army had pushed back rebel forces who tried to advance from the north east.

"Heavy fighting took place yesterday on the road to Bafwasende. There was an attempt by the rebels to breach our lines. The army killed 35 of them and pushed them back," a spokesman said on Wednesday.

Earlier, France told the U.N. Human Rights Commission that the outside world must intervene to protect the refugees as well as Zairean civilians and called for a multi-national force to be sent if the rebels refused to agree a truce.
